class quantx_engine.LogicalQubit(distance, physical_error_rate=0.001, rng_seed=None)[source]¶

Bases: object

A logical qubit encoded in a distance-d repetition code.

The repetition code encodes one logical qubit in d physical qubits with the logical operators L_X = X⊗X⊗…⊗X and L_Z = Z⊗I⊗…⊗I. It corrects ⌊(d−1)/2⌋ single-qubit Z errors.

Parameters:

  • distance (int) – Code distance (must be odd, ≥ 3).

  • physical_error_rate (float) – Per-physical-qubit error rate (probability of a single-qubit Z flip per syndrome measurement round).

  • rng_seed (int, optional) – Seed for reproducible simulations.

distance: int¶
physical_error_rate: float = 0.001¶
rng_seed: int | None = None¶
property n_physical: int¶

Number of physical qubits.

property t_correctable: int¶

Number of Z errors correctable per round.

property logical_state: int¶

Current logical state (0 or 1) accounting for Pauli frame.

encode(state=0)[source]¶

Encode logical |state⟩ (0 or 1).

measure_z(*, n_rounds=1)[source]¶

Measure the logical qubit in the Z basis with error correction.

Simulates n_rounds of syndrome measurement under a depolarising noise model and applies majority-vote correction. The call projects the qubit onto the measured eigenstate.

Returns:

0 or 1 (logical measurement outcome after correction).

Return type:

int

class quantx_engine.MagicStateDistillery(p_in=0.01, rng_seed=None)[source]¶

Bases: object

15-to-1 magic state distillation for fault-tolerant T gates.

The 15-to-1 protocol (Bravyi & Kitaev 2005) takes 15 noisy |T⟩ states with input error rate p_in and outputs one |T⟩ state with error rate approximately 35·p_in³.

Parameters:

  • p_in (float) – Input |T⟩ state error rate (probability that a state is |T̄⟩ = Z|T⟩).

  • rng_seed (int, optional)

p_in: float = 0.01¶
rng_seed: int | None = None¶
property p_out_theoretical: float¶

Theoretical output error rate ≈ 35·p_in³.

distill_one()[source]¶

Run one 15-to-1 distillation attempt.

Returns:

0 if distillation succeeded (high-fidelity |T⟩ accepted), 1 if the output state is an error, None if post-selection rejected the attempt (error detected).

Return type:

int or None

class quantx_engine.CrosstalkModel(system, graph)[source]¶

Bases: object

Idle Hamiltonian evolution including ZZ crosstalk.

Adds H_ZZ to the static rotating-frame Hamiltonian of a QubitSystem and simulates idle evolution.

Parameters:

  • system (QubitSystem)

  • graph (CouplingGraph) – ZZ coupling strengths. Must have the same n_qubits.

__init__(system, graph)[source]¶
zz_phase(q0, q1, idle_time)[source]¶

Accumulated ZZ phase (rad) between q0 and q1 during an idle period.

φ_ZZ = ζ_{q0,q1} · idle_time

idle_unitary(idle_time)[source]¶

Exact unitary U = exp(−i (H₀ + H_ZZ) · idle_time).

evolve_idle(idle_time, initial_state=None)[source]¶

Simulate idle evolution (no drive) for idle_time.

Uses the exact matrix exponential rather than ODE integration for efficiency.

Parameters:

  • idle_time (float)

  • initial_state (array of shape (2^n,), optional) – Defaults to |0…0⟩.

Returns:

Populations and final state after idle evolution.

Return type:

PulseResult

quantx_engine.zz_routing_cost(graph, q0, q1, *, swap_base_cost=1.0, zz_weight=1.0)[source]¶

SABRE-compatible edge cost that penalises high-ZZ pairs.

Cost = swap_base_cost + zz_weight · |ζ_{q0,q1}|

A router minimising this cost prefers to route through low-ZZ neighbours, reducing idle crosstalk accumulated during SWAP decomposition.

Parameters:

  • graph (CouplingGraph)

  • q0 (int) – Candidate SWAP edge.

  • q1 (int) – Candidate SWAP edge.

  • swap_base_cost (float) – Fixed cost per SWAP (default 1.0).

  • zz_weight (float) – Scaling factor for the ZZ penalty (default 1.0).

Returns:

Edge cost ≥ swap_base_cost.

Return type:

float

quantx_engine.cheapest_path(graph, source, target, *, swap_base_cost=1.0, zz_weight=1.0)[source]¶

Dijkstra shortest path minimising zz_routing_cost().

Returns:

(path, total_cost) – path is the ordered list of qubit indices from source to target (inclusive). Returns ([], inf) if no path exists.

Return type:

(list[int], float)

quantx_engine.echo_sequence(q0, q1, idle_time, *, pi_duration=20.0, pi_sigma=None, use_gaussian=False)[source]¶

Build an X–X refocusing echo schedule to cancel ZZ accumulation.

The sequence is:

idle(T/2) – X(q0)·X(q1) – idle(T/2)

The two X pulses at T/2 flip both qubits simultaneously, reversing the sign of the ZZ phase so that the net ZZ accumulation cancels to zero.

Parameters:

  • q0 (int) – Qubit indices to echo.

  • q1 (int) – Qubit indices to echo.

  • idle_time (float) – Total idle period to refocus.

  • pi_duration (float) – Duration of the π-pulse (used as T for ConstantWaveform or duration for GaussianWaveform).

  • pi_sigma (float, optional) – Gaussian σ. Required when use_gaussian is True.

  • use_gaussian (bool) – If True use GaussianWaveform; otherwise use ConstantWaveform.

Returns:

Schedule of total duration idle_time + pi_duration.

Return type:

PulseSchedule

class quantx_engine.DRAGWaveform(duration, amp, sigma, beta)[source]¶

Bases: Waveform

DRAG (Derivative Removal via Adiabatic Gate) waveform.

In-phase component : Gaussian envelope I(t). Quadrature component: Q(t) = −beta · dI/dt.

Returns a complex envelope I(t) + i·Q(t). With beta tuned to the qubit anharmonicity this suppresses leakage to |2⟩.

class quantx_engine.QubitSystem(n_qubits, frequencies, drive_frequencies=None, t1_times=None, t2_times=None, coupling_map=None)[source]¶

Bases: object

Describes the physical multi-qubit Hamiltonian and noise parameters.

Parameters:

  • n_qubits (int)

  • frequencies (list[float]) – Qubit transition frequencies ω_j (angular, same unit as waveform amplitudes).

  • drive_frequencies (list[float] | None) – LO frequencies ω_drive_j. Defaults to frequencies (on-resonance).

  • t1_times (list[float] | None) – Amplitude-damping times T1_j. None or 0 means no T1 noise on that qubit.

  • t2_times (list[float] | None) – Total dephasing times T2_j (T2 ≤ 2·T1).

  • coupling_map (list[tuple[int, int, float]] | None) – Exchange couplings [(q0, q1, J), …] added as J(σ+_q0 σ-_q1 + h.c.).

class quantx_engine.PulseSimulator(method='RK45', atol=1e-08, rtol=1e-06, record_states=False, n_record_points=50)[source]¶

Bases: object

Pulse-level simulator based on scipy.integrate.solve_ivp().

Pure state (no T1/T2 in QubitSystem): solves the time-dependent Schrödinger equation.

Open system (T1 and/or T2 specified): solves the Lindblad master equation on the density matrix.

quantx_engine.pi_pulse_area(sigma)[source]¶

Return the Gaussian amplitude that gives a π-rotation for the given σ.

For H(t) = Ω(t)/2 · σx, the π condition is ∫ Ω dt = π. Gaussian area = amp · σ · √(2π), so amp = π / (σ · √(2π)).

static pybind11_available()[source]¶

Return True when the pybind11 extension module _quantx_py is loaded.

When True, run_statevector() and run_circuit_sv() avoid the JSON serialisation overhead and return NumPy arrays via a direct C++→Python memory copy.

run_statevector(problem, options=None)[source]¶

Run a Hamiltonian simulation and return the statevector.

When the pybind11 extension is available (pybind11_available() is True), this method returns a numpy.ndarray of dtype complex128 with shape (2**n_qubits,) — no JSON serialisation is performed.

Without pybind11 the result falls back to the ctypes JSON path and the statevector is returned as a list of [re, im] pairs embedded in the normal result dict under the "state" key.

Parameters:

  • problem (dict) – Problem specification (same schema as run()).

  • options (dict, optional) – Runtime options.

Returns:

NumPy array via pybind11, or full result dict via ctypes fallback.

Return type:

numpy.ndarray (complex128) or dict

run_circuit_sv(circuit)[source]¶

Execute a gate-level circuit and return the output statevector.

When the pybind11 extension is available, this returns a numpy.ndarray[complex128] directly. Otherwise it calls the ctypes path and returns the full result dict.

Parameters:

circuit (dict) – Circuit payload (same schema as run_circuit()).

Return type:

numpy.ndarray (complex128) or dict

run_circuit_counts_np(circuit)[source]¶

Execute a gate-level circuit and return measurement counts.

When pybind11 is available, the counts dict is populated directly from C++ (no JSON round-trip). Otherwise this is equivalent to calling run_circuit(circuit).get("counts", {}).

Parameters:

circuit (dict)

Return type:

dict[str, int]

exception quantx_engine.QuantXNativeUnavailable[source]¶

Bases: RuntimeError

Raised when the native QuantX shared library cannot be loaded.

This happens when quantx-engine is installed as a pure-Python wheel (no C++ build) or when the library path is incorrect. All pure-Python modules — simulators, chemistry solvers, error-correction codes, etc. — continue to work normally; only features that call through to the native C++ engine require the library.

class quantx_engine.DepolarizingNoise(prob)[source]¶

Bases: NoiseModel

Uniform depolarizing channel applied after every gate.

The depolarizing channel replaces the qubit state with the maximally mixed state with probability p: ρ → (1-p)ρ + p·I/2, which is (1 - 3p/4)ρ + (p/4)(XρX + YρY + ZρZ). The native circuit backend applies it to every qubit after every gate (idle qubits included), one trajectory per shot. The density-matrix simulator in quantx_engine.primitives and the dynamic-circuit simulator apply it the same way (see native_channels()).

Parameters:

prob (float) – Depolarizing probability per gate, in [0, 1].

class quantx_engine.ThermalRelaxationNoise(T1, T2, t_gate=50.0)[source]¶

Bases: NoiseModel

Combined T1/T2 thermal relaxation noise model.

Computes amplitude damping γ = 1 − exp(−t_gate / T1) from the longitudinal relaxation time T1 and gate duration t_gate. The T2 dephasing parameter λ = 1 − exp(−t_gate / T2) is computed and stored in the output dict under noise_metadata for informational purposes, but is not currently consumed by the native circuit backend (which supports T1 amplitude damping only via the t1_decay noise kind).

to_dict() emits {"noise": {"kind": "t1_decay", "T1": T1, "dt": t_gate}, "noise_metadata": {...}} — only the noise sub-dict is executed.

The constraint T2 ≤ 2·T1 (Lindblad bound) is enforced.

Parameters:

  • T1 (float) – Longitudinal relaxation time in nanoseconds.

  • T2 (float) – Transverse relaxation time in nanoseconds. Must satisfy T2 ≤ 2·T1.

  • t_gate (float) – Gate duration in nanoseconds (default: 50 ns, typical for superconducting qubits).

class quantx_engine.ReadoutNoise(prob)[source]¶

Bases: NoiseModel

Symmetric bit-flip noise, intended to stand in for readout errors.

The native circuit backend implements this as a bit_flip channel (noise = {"kind": "bit_flip", "prob": p}): after every gate except a measurement, each qubit flips with probability p. So it acts as gate noise, not as a readout error. A true readout error model would act on the measurement outcomes only; bit_flip is the closest mechanism the backend supports.

Parameters:

prob (float) – Bit-flip probability per qubit per gate, in [0, 0.5]. Values above 0.5 are anti-correlated and should be modeled differently.

__init__(prob)[source]¶
property prob: float¶
to_dict()[source]¶

Return the JSON-serializable noise payload for Engine.run_circuit().

class quantx_engine.CompositeNoise(models)[source]¶

Bases: NoiseModel

Combination of multiple noise models applied simultaneously.

to_dict() is the union of the models’ payloads, so the models must emit disjoint keys. If two models emit the same key, building the composite (constructor or +) raises NoiseModelError; no entry is ever silently replaced.

In practice this allows at most one noise-kind model per composite. ThermalRelaxationNoise (t1_decay) and ReadoutNoise (bit_flip) both put their channel under the single key noise, because the native backend parses exactly one noise object per circuit (parse_noise_config in src/json_utils.cpp). A second one has no slot to go to: merging the two would drop a channel. DepolarizingNoise and AmplitudeDampingNoise emit the top-level fields depolarizing_prob and amplitude_damping_gamma, which the backend applies alongside the noise channel, so they combine with each other and with one noise-kind model:

CompositeNoise([DepolarizingNoise(0.005),
                ThermalRelaxationNoise(T1=1e5, T2=6e4, t_gate=50)])  # ok
CompositeNoise([ThermalRelaxationNoise(T1=1e5, T2=6e4, t_gate=50),
                ReadoutNoise(0.02)])     # NoiseModelError: both emit "noise"

Every key is checked, not only noise. Each top-level field holds one value per circuit, so two DepolarizingNoise models collide on depolarizing_prob (build one model instead). noise_metadata is checked as well: no simulator executes it, but a merge would keep only one model’s description.

The check is on the fields a payload sets, not only on its keys. A noise selector of kind depolarizing or amplitude_damping (no shipped model emits one, but the backend accepts both, so a custom model may) is another spelling of depolarizing_prob or amplitude_damping_gamma: the backend writes its prob or gamma (at the selector’s top level or in its params) into that field. Such a selector therefore collides with a DepolarizingNoise or AmplitudeDampingNoise although the keys differ. A selector that carries no value leaves the field alone, and combines.

Parameters:

models (list[NoiseModel]) – List of NoiseModel instances to combine.

Raises:

NoiseModelError – If models is empty, holds a non-NoiseModel, or two models set the same field: they emit the same key, or one emits a noise selector that the backend writes into another’s field.

__init__(models)[source]¶
property models: list[NoiseModel]¶
to_dict()[source]¶

Return the JSON-serializable noise payload for Engine.run_circuit().

quantx_engine.jordan_wigner(one_body, two_body, n_orbitals, constant=0.0)[source]¶

Apply the Jordan-Wigner transform to a second-quantized Hamiltonian.

H = constant + Σ h_pq a†_p a_q + ½ Σ g_pqrs a†_p a†_q a_r a_s

Each fermionic mode p maps to qubit p via:

a†_p = (X_p - iY_p)/2 × Z_0 ⊗ … ⊗ Z_{p-1} a_p = (X_p + iY_p)/2 × Z_0 ⊗ … ⊗ Z_{p-1}

Parameters:

  • one_body (list[tuple[int, int, float]]) – List of (p, q, h_pq) tuples for one-body integrals.

  • two_body (list[tuple[int, int, int, int, float]]) – List of (p, q, r, s, g_pqrs) tuples for two-body integrals (physicist notation: ⟨pq|rs⟩).

  • n_orbitals (int) – Number of spin-orbitals (= 2 × spatial orbitals for spin ½).

  • constant (float) – Nuclear repulsion / constant energy shift.

Returns:

Qubit Hamiltonian in the Pauli basis.

Return type:

PauliHamiltonian

quantx_engine.hf_state(n_electrons, n_qubits)[source]¶

Return the Hartree-Fock reference state vector.

The HF state occupies the n_electrons lowest-indexed spin-orbitals. Qubit 0 is the most significant (leftmost) tensor factor, so the occupied qubits 0..n_electrons-1 give index 2ⁿ − 2^(n-n_e) = ... = integer with the top n_e bits set.

Parameters:

  • n_electrons (int) – Number of electrons (occupied spin-orbitals).

  • n_qubits (int) – Total number of spin-orbitals / qubits.

Return type:

numpy.ndarray of shape (2**n_qubits,), dtype complex128.

class quantx_engine.UCCSDSolver(n_electrons, n_qubits)[source]¶

Bases: object

Unitary Coupled Cluster Singles and Doubles solver.

Builds the UCCSD ansatz by:

  1. Generating all single-excitation generators K_single = a†_v a_o − h.c. and double-excitation generators K_double = a†_v₁ a†_v₂ a_o₂ a_o₁ − h.c. in the Jordan-Wigner representation.

  2. Forming the combined anti-Hermitian operator A(θ) = Σ θ_s K_s + Σ θ_d K_d.

  3. Preparing the UCCSD state |ψ(θ)⟩ = expm(A(θ)) |HF⟩ via exact matrix exponentiation.

  4. Minimizing ⟨ψ(θ)|H|ψ(θ)⟩ over θ using coordinate descent.

Parameters:

  • n_electrons (int) – Number of electrons (occupied spin-orbitals in HF reference).

  • n_qubits (int) – Total number of spin-orbitals / qubits.

Examples

>>> from quantx_engine.chemistry import MolecularVQE
>>> from quantx_engine.advanced_chemistry import UCCSDSolver, build_hamiltonian_matrix
>>> problem = MolecularVQE.h2()
>>> H = build_hamiltonian_matrix(problem.hamiltonian)
>>> result = UCCSDSolver(n_electrons=2, n_qubits=4).run(H)
>>> abs(result.energy - problem.fci_energy) < 0.01
True
__init__(n_electrons, n_qubits)[source]¶

class quantx_engine.ADAPTVQESolver(n_electrons, n_qubits, pool=None)[source]¶

Bases: object

Adaptive derivative-assembled pseudo-Trotter VQE (ADAPT-VQE).

At each iteration, finds the operator from the pool with the largest energy gradient and appends it to the ansatz with a new parameter. Stops when the maximum absolute gradient falls below threshold or max_operators is reached.

Parameters:

  • n_electrons (int) – Number of electrons in the HF reference.

  • n_qubits (int) – Total number of qubits.

  • pool (list[np.ndarray] | None) – List of anti-Hermitian generator matrices. If None, uses the UCCSD pool (all singles + doubles).

class quantx_engine.QAOASolver(n_qubits)[source]¶

Bases: object

Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm.

Prepares the p-layer QAOA state:

|ψ(γ,β)⟩ = ∏_{l=1}^{p} exp(-iβ_l H_B) exp(-iγ_l H_C) |+⟩^⊗n

where H_B = Σ_i X_i is the mixer Hamiltonian and H_C is the cost Hamiltonian. Optimizes ⟨ψ(γ,β)|H_C|ψ(γ,β)⟩ over the 2p parameters.

Parameters:

n_qubits (int) – Number of qubits.

class quantx_engine.QITESolver(n_qubits)[source]¶

Bases: object

Quantum Imaginary Time Evolution (QITE).

Evolves an initial state under:

|ψ(τ + Δτ)⟩ ∝ (I − ΔτH) |ψ(τ)⟩

which converges to the ground state of H as τ → ∞.

Parameters:

n_qubits (int) – Number of qubits.

Examples

>>> H = build_hamiltonian_matrix(MolecularVQE.h2().hamiltonian)
>>> result = QITESolver(n_qubits=4).run(H, delta_tau=0.05, n_steps=100)
>>> result.final_energy  # close to FCI energy -1.1373

class quantx_engine.ZZFeatureMap(n_qubits, n_reps=2)[source]¶

Bases: QuantumFeatureMap

ZZ-entanglement circuit feature map (IBM Qiskit convention).

Each of n_reps repetitions applies:

  1. Hadamard on every qubit: H^⊗n

  2. Phase encoding: Rz(2 x_i) on qubit i for all i

  3. Pairwise ZZ interactions for all ordered pairs (i, j), i < j:

    CX_{i,j} → Rz_j(2(π − x_i)(π − x_j)) → CX_{i,j}

This realises the unitary U_φ(x) such that |φ(x)⟩ = U_φ(x)|0…0⟩.

Parameters:

  • n_qubits (int) – Number of qubits (must equal the dimension of the input vectors).

  • n_reps (int) – Number of encoding layers.

class quantx_engine.FidelityQuantumKernel(feature_map)[source]¶

Bases: object

Fidelity (overlap) quantum kernel.

K(x, x’) = |⟨φ(x)|φ(x’)⟩|²

The diagonal satisfies K(x, x) = 1 for any unit-normalised feature map. The kernel matrix is positive semi-definite by construction.

  • Y (ndarray | None) – Array of shape (n_y, n_features). If None, computes the symmetric self-kernel of X (exploiting K[i,j] = K[j,i]).

Returns:

  • Y is None), entries in [0, 1].

ndarray

quantx_engine.target_alignment(K, y)[source]¶

Kernel-Target Alignment (KTA) between kernel K and labels y.

Measures how well K separates the two classes:

KTA = ⟨K, yy^T⟩_F / (n · ‖K‖_F)

where ⟨·,·⟩_F is the Frobenius inner product and y ∈ {−1, +1}. KTA = 1 when K = yy^T (perfect alignment).

Parameters:

  • K (ndarray) – Kernel matrix of shape (n, n).

  • y (ndarray) – Binary labels ±1, shape (n,).

Return type:

float in [−1, 1] (0 for trivial/zero kernel).

quantx_engine.frobenius_alignment(K1, K2)[source]¶

Cosine similarity between two kernel matrices in Frobenius norm.

Returns ⟨K1, K2⟩_F / (‖K1‖_F · ‖K2‖_F).

Parameters:

  • K1 (ndarray) – Kernel matrices of the same shape.

  • K2 (ndarray) – Kernel matrices of the same shape.

Return type:

float in [−1, 1] (0 if either matrix is zero).

class quantx_engine.QSVM(feature_map=None, kernel=None, C=1.0)[source]¶

Bases: object

Quantum Support Vector Machine for binary classification.

Trains a soft-margin SVM using the fidelity quantum kernel:

K(x, x') = |⟨φ(x)|φ(x')⟩|²

The dual QP is solved with a simplified Sequential Minimal Optimisation (SMO) algorithm.

Parameters:

  • feature_map (QuantumFeatureMap | None) – A QuantumFeatureMap instance. Exactly one of feature_map or kernel must be supplied.

  • kernel (FidelityQuantumKernel | None) – A pre-built FidelityQuantumKernel. Takes precedence over feature_map when both are given.

  • C (float) – Soft-margin regularisation parameter (must be > 0). Larger C allows fewer margin violations.

Examples

>>> fm  = ZZFeatureMap(n_qubits=2, n_reps=1)
>>> clf = QSVM(feature_map=fm, C=1.0)
>>> X   = np.array([[0.1, 0.2], [0.9, 0.8]])
>>> y   = np.array([-1.0, 1.0])
>>> result = clf.fit(X, y)
>>> clf.predict(np.array([[0.15, 0.15]]))[0] in {-1.0, 1.0}
True

class quantx_engine.StandardRB(n_qubits=1, p_error=0.001, seed=None, *, gate_error=None)[source]¶

Bases: object

Standard randomized benchmarking.

Generates random Clifford sequences of lengths m, appends the composite inverse, and estimates the survival probability via exact density-matrix simulation with a global depolarizing channel.

Currently supports 1-qubit RB using the full 24-element Clifford group and n-qubit RB using Haar-random unitaries (approximate RB).

Parameters:

  • n_qubits (int) – Number of qubits (1 for standard single-qubit RB).

  • p_error (float) – Depolarizing error probability per Clifford gate. 0 = noiseless.

  • seed (int | None) – Optional random seed for reproducibility.

IBM Quantum Volume protocol.

class quantx_engine.QuantumNeuralNetwork(n_qubits, n_layers=2, n_outputs=1, backend='numpy')[source]¶

Bases: object

Parameterized quantum circuit for supervised learning.

The circuit uses angle encoding followed by hardware-efficient ansatz layers. Gradients are computed exactly via the parameter-shift rule. State evolution is handled by GpuStatevector, so passing backend="cupy" transparently enables GPU acceleration.

Parameters:

  • n_qubits (int) – Number of qubits. Must be >= n_features if you want full encoding; features beyond n_qubits are truncated.

  • n_layers (int) – Number of ansatz repetitions (depth = n_layers * (n_qubits + n_qubits - 1)).

  • n_outputs (int) – Number of output nodes (qubits measured). 1 for binary classification.

  • backend (str) – Statevector backend: "numpy" (default), "cupy", or "auto".

class quantx_engine.RepetitionCode(n)[source]¶

Bases: object

[[n, 1, n]] repetition code (odd n recommended).

Encodes one logical qubit into n physical qubits. Protects against ⌊(n-1)/2⌋ bit-flip (Z-basis) errors. Phase-flip errors are undetected.

Parameters:

n (int) – Number of physical qubits. Use odd n for symmetric correction.

Encode logical 0 or 1 into n physical qubits.

Physical codeword, list of n bits.

Compute parity-check syndrome of a (possibly errored) codeword.

  • Syndrome bits (1 where Z_i Z_{i+1} anticommutes (a parity flip), else 0.)

  • Length = n-1.

Return type:

list[int]

decode(codeword)[source]¶

Majority-vote decoder: return the most common bit value.

Optimal for independent, identically distributed bit-flip errors with p < 0.5.

Decoded logical bit (0 or 1).

correct(codeword)[source]¶

Apply syndrome-based correction and return the corrected codeword.

Uses the first non-zero syndrome pair to identify the error location. Handles single errors exactly; applies greedy correction for multiple.

Bases: object

Minimum-Weight Perfect Matching decoder for stabilizer codes (M78).

Uses an exact bitmask-DP MWPM solver for small syndrome sizes and a greedy nearest-neighbour fallback for larger ones. The syndrome graph infrastructure from SurfaceCode is reused directly, so the decoder is compatible with any code that exposes _build_syndrome_graph, _syndrome_graph_bfs, z_stabs, x_stabs, and n.

Unlike the built-in greedy decoder in SurfaceCode, MWPM finds the globally optimal correction (minimum total edge weight), which reduces the logical error rate — especially at low physical error rates.

Parameters:

  • code (SurfaceCode | RepetitionCode) – A SurfaceCode or RepetitionCode instance.

  • max_exact (int) – Maximum number of actual defects for which the exact bitmask-DP solver is used. The DP operates on 2 * n_defects nodes; the default of 10 defects corresponds to 20 DP nodes, which runs in ~20 ms. For larger syndrome sizes the greedy fallback is used.

Examples

>>> code = SurfaceCode(d=5)
>>> decoder = MWPMDecoder(code)
>>> x_errors = [0] * 25
>>> x_errors[3] = 1
>>> syn = code.z_syndrome(x_errors)
>>> correction = decoder.decode_x(syn)
__init__(code, max_exact=10)[source]¶

Transverse-field Ising MPO: H = -J Σ Z_i Z_{i+1} − h Σ X_i.

Second-order Suzuki-Trotter evolution under H = -J Σ ZZ − h Σ X.

solve_heisenberg(n_sites, J=1.0, Jz=1.0, h=0.0)[source]¶

Find lowest k eigenpairs of the 1D Heisenberg chain.

Routes through the native C++ Heisenberg solver when the QuantX native library is available (QUANTX_LIB_PATH is set), giving ≥10× speedup for n_sites ≥ 10. Falls back transparently to the pure-Python Lanczos algorithm otherwise.

Parameters:

  • n_sites (int) – Number of spin-½ sites (Hilbert-space dimension = 2^n_sites).

  • J (float) – Transverse exchange coupling (XX + YY part, scaled by J/2 in the Hamiltonian).

  • Jz (float) – Longitudinal exchange (ZZ part). Jz = J → isotropic Heisenberg.

  • h (float) – Uniform longitudinal field h Σ Z_i.

Returns:

Eigenvalues are in ascending order; at most self.k values are returned (may be fewer if the Hilbert space is small).

Return type:

EigenResult

static ising_1d(n_sites, J=1.0, h=0.5)[source]¶

1D transverse-field Ising H = -J sum ZiZi+1 - h sum Xi (periodic BC).

Hilbert space: 2^n_sites, basis states |s0 s1 … s_{n-1}>, si in {0,1}. State index: i = s0 + 2*s1 + 4*s2 + …

static heisenberg_1d(n_sites, J=1.0, hz=0.0)[source]¶

1D Heisenberg H = J sum (Xi Xi+1 + Yi Yi+1 + Zi Zi+1) + hz sum Zi (open BC).

XX+YY = 2(S+S- + S-S+): flips adjacent antiparallel spins. ZZ: diagonal. For spin-1/2: S+|0>=|1>, S+|1>=0; S-|1>=|0>, S-|0>=0 (|0>=up, |1>=down). Xi Xi+1 + Yi Yi+1 = 2(S+i S-i+1 + S-i S+i+1) where S+/- = sigma+/-/2. Matrix element for antiparallel flip: J * 0.5.

static from_pauli_terms(n_sites, terms)[source]¶

Build a SparseHamiltonian from a list of Pauli-string terms.

Each term is a (coefficient, ops, sites) triple where:

  • coefficient — real or complex scalar prefactor.

  • ops — string of single-character Pauli labels, one per site (e.g. "ZZ", "XY", "Z"). Supported: 'I', 'X', 'Y', 'Z'.

  • sites — list of qubit indices, same length as ops.

The Hamiltonian acts on a 2ⁿ-dimensional Hilbert space with the computational basis ordered as \(|s_0, s_1, \ldots, s_{n-1}\rangle\) where \(s_i = (\text{state} >> i) \& 1\).

Parameters:

  • n_sites (int) – Number of qubits.

  • terms (list[tuple[float | complex, str, list[int]]]) – List of (coefficient, ops, sites) tuples.

Return type:

SparseHamiltonian

Examples

Reproduce a 3-site ZZ + transverse-field Ising model:

H = SparseHamiltonian.from_pauli_terms(3, [
    (-1.0, "ZZ", [0, 1]),
    (-1.0, "ZZ", [1, 2]),
    (-0.5, "X",  [0]),
    (-0.5, "X",  [1]),
    (-0.5, "X",  [2]),
])
static xxz_chain(n_sites, J=1.0, delta=1.0, hz=0.0)[source]¶

1D XXZ spin chain (open BC).

\[H = J \sum_{i=0}^{n-2} \left[ \frac{1}{2}(\sigma^+_i \sigma^-_{i+1} + \text{h.c.}) + \Delta\, Z_i Z_{i+1} \right] + h_z \sum_i Z_i\]

where \(\sigma^+ = \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\), J is the overall exchange scale, and delta (Δ) is the anisotropy ratio.

Special cases:

  • delta=1: isotropic Heisenberg antiferromagnet; xxz_chain(n, J=J, delta=1) equals heisenberg_1d(n, J=J)

  • delta=0: XX model (free-fermion), no ZZ coupling

  • delta→∞: classical Ising limit

Parameters:

  • n_sites (int) – Number of spins. Must be >= 1.

  • J (float) – Overall exchange coupling (energy scale).

  • delta (float) – Anisotropy Δ = J_z / J_xy.

  • hz (float) – Uniform longitudinal field.

static heisenberg_2d(Lx, Ly, J=1.0)[source]¶

2D Heisenberg model on an Lx × Ly rectangular lattice (open BC).

\[H = J \sum_{\langle ij \rangle} \left[ Z_i Z_j + \frac{1}{2}(\sigma^+_i \sigma^-_j + \text{h.c.}) \right]\]

Sites are labelled (x, y) → x + y·Lx. Bonds connect (x, y)–(x+1, y) (horizontal) and (x, y)–(x, y+1) (vertical).

Parameters:

  • Lx (int) – Lattice dimensions. Total sites = Lx * Ly ≤ 20 (dense backend).

  • Ly (int) – Lattice dimensions. Total sites = Lx * Ly ≤ 20 (dense backend).

  • J (float) – Exchange coupling.

static bose_hubbard(L, t=1.0, U=4.0, max_occ=4)[source]¶

Bose-Hubbard model on a 1D chain (open BC).

\[H = -t \sum_i (a^\dagger_i a_{i+1} + \text{h.c.}) + \frac{U}{2} \sum_i n_i(n_i - 1)\]

Fock basis: each site holds 0 … max_occ bosons. State index:

\[\text{idx} = \sum_{i=0}^{L-1} n_i \cdot M^i, \quad M = \text{max\_occ} + 1\]

Hilbert space dimension: (max_occ + 1)^L.

Parameters:

  • L (int) – Number of sites.

  • t (float) – Hopping amplitude.

  • U (float) – On-site interaction strength.

  • max_occ (int) – Maximum occupation per site (truncation).

static hubbard_1d(L, t=1.0, U=4.0)[source]¶

Single-band Fermi-Hubbard model on a 1D chain (open BC).

\[H = -t \sum_{i,\sigma} (c^\dagger_{i,\sigma} c_{i+1,\sigma} + \text{h.c.}) + U \sum_i n_{i,\uparrow} n_{i,\downarrow}\]

Encoding: spin-up occupations in the lower L bits (bit i = site i spin-up), spin-down occupations in the upper L bits. State index: up_bits | (down_bits << L). Hilbert space dimension: 4^L = 2^{2L}.

JW ordering — (\uparrow_0, \uparrow_1, \ldots, \downarrow_0, \downarrow_1, \ldots) — gives sign +1 for nearest-neighbour intra-sector hopping.

Parameters:

  • L (int) – Number of sites.

  • t (float) – Hopping amplitude.

  • U (float) – On-site Hubbard interaction.

class quantx_engine.SteadyStateSolver(tol=1e-08, *, H=None, jump_operators=None)[source]¶

Bases: object

Find a fixed point ρ_ss of a quantum channel: Φ(ρ_ss) = ρ_ss.

Algorithm:

  1. Build the Liouville superoperator L = Σ K_n ⊗ K_n*.

  2. Find eigenvalues/vectors of L.

  3. Among eigenvectors with eigenvalue closest to 1, select the one whose reshaped matrix is most positive (smallest negative eigenvalue mass).

  4. Project to Hermitian, project to PSD, normalise trace to 1.

For CPTP maps the eigenvalue 1 is always present; the corresponding eigenvector(s) span the set of fixed points.

Note

For channels with a degenerate fixed-point subspace (e.g. the identity channel, or p = 0 dephasing) the solver returns one valid fixed-point density matrix. The result is determined by the eigenvector ordering from numpy.linalg.eig() and is not guaranteed to be a specific state. If you need all fixed points, compute the nullspace of (L − I) manually.

Parameters:

tol (float) – Threshold for identifying eigenvalues as “equal to 1”.

__init__(tol=1e-08, *, H=None, jump_operators=None)[source]¶

Returns:

Density matrix ρ_ss of shape (d, d): Hermitian, PSD, trace = 1, satisfying Φ(ρ_ss) ≈ ρ_ss.

Return type:

np.ndarray

Raises:

ChannelError – If no physically valid fixed point can be found.

Bases: object

Finite-size scaling analysis for quantum phase transitions.

Identifies the critical coupling J_c where Binder cumulant curves for different system sizes L cross, using linear interpolation of adjacent-size pairs.

Raises:

Find crossing points of consecutive Binder cumulant curves.

For each adjacent pair (L_i, L_{i+1}) finds the parameter value where U_{L_i}(J) = U_{L_{i+1}}(J) using linear interpolation.

Returns:

Crossing parameter values, one per consecutive pair that has a crossing in the supplied range. May be empty.

list[float]

Estimate the critical coupling from Binder cumulant crossings.

critical_point = mean of crossing estimates; critical_point_std = standard deviation (0.0 if only one crossing is found).

Return type:

ScalingResult

data_collapse(jc, nu, observable=None, beta_over_nu=0.0)[source]¶

Measure data-collapse quality for given (J_c, ν).

Rescales the parameter axis as x̃ = (J − J_c) · L^{1/ν} and (if observable and beta_over_nu are provided) the observable axis as Ỹ = O · L^{β/ν}, then computes the mean-squared distance between adjacent rescaled curves (interpolated onto a common grid).

A perfect collapse gives cost = 0.

Parameters:

  • jc (float) – Trial critical coupling.

  • nu (float) – Trial correlation-length exponent (must be > 0).

  • observable (ndarray | None) – 2D array (n_sizes, n_params) of order-parameter values. If None, the Binder cumulant is used (and β/ν = 0).

  • beta_over_nu (float) – β/ν exponent for y-axis rescaling. Use 0 for Binder cumulant.

Returns:

Mean squared deviation averaged over all N(N−1)/2 unique pairs of rescaled curves (not just adjacent pairs). Using all pairs makes the metric more robust when sizes span a wide range. Lower is better. Returns float('inf') if no pair has an overlapping rescaled-x region with at least 2 points; this can happen when jc is far outside the supplied parameter range or nu is very small.

Return type:

float

Raises:

FiniteSizeError – If nu <= 0 or observable has wrong shape.

quantx_engine.binder_cumulant(samples)[source]¶

Compute the Binder cumulant U = 1 − ⟨m⁴⟩ / (3⟨m²⟩²).

The Binder cumulant is a dimensionless ratio that distinguishes phases without needing the thermodynamic limit:

  • U → 0 disordered phase (Gaussian fluctuations: ⟨m⁴⟩ = 3⟨m²⟩²)

  • U → 2/3 ordered phase (bimodal: |m| ≈ const)

At the critical point, Binder cumulant curves for different system sizes L cross at a universal value U* ∈ (0, 2/3).

Note

This function uses raw moments ⟨m²⟩ and ⟨m⁴⟩ (the standard definition in the condensed-matter literature). These are not centred cumulants. Passing samples with a non-zero mean correctly gives U ≈ 2/3 for a biased ordered phase (e.g. ferromagnet in an external field), which is the physically correct result.

Parameters:

samples (ndarray) – 1D (or ravelled) array of order-parameter values. At least 2 samples are required.

Returns:

Binder cumulant U. Theoretically in [0, 2/3], but may be slightly outside this range due to finite sampling.

Return type:

float

Raises:

FiniteSizeError – If fewer than 2 samples are provided or ⟨m²⟩ ≈ 0.

quantx_engine.entanglement_scaling(psi, L, d=2)[source]¶

Compute bipartite von Neumann entropy S(A) for all bipartitions.

Reshapes the length-d^L state vector as a (d^A, d^{L−A}) matrix and computes the von Neumann entropy

S(A) = −Tr(ρ_A ln ρ_A) = −∑_i λ_i ln λ_i,

where λ_i = σ_i² are the eigenvalues of the reduced density matrix ρ_A obtained from the singular values σ_i of the reshaped matrix.

For a 1D critical system described by a CFT with central charge c, the entropy satisfies

S(A) = (c/3) ln[(L/π) sin(πA/L)] + s₀.

A least-squares fit of this formula (for L ≥ 4) returns the central charge.

Parameters:

  • psi (ndarray) –

    State vector, shape (d^L,). Must be exactly d^L elements. Need not be normalised (normalisation is applied internally).

    Storage convention: the state is indexed in standard tensor-product (row-major / C) order, i.e. psi[i] = ⟨s_0 s_1 … s_{L-1}|ψ⟩ where site 0 is the most-significant index. Equivalently, index = s_0·d^{L-1} + s_1·d^{L-2} + … + s_{L-1}. This is the natural NumPy ordering and the convention used throughout QuantX.

  • L (int) – Number of lattice sites.

  • d (int) – Local Hilbert-space dimension (default 2 for qubits/spin-1/2).

Return type:

EntanglementResult

Raises:

FiniteSizeError – If len(psi) != d^L or psi has near-zero norm.

class quantx_engine.KrylovEvolver(m=30, dt=0.1, *, H=None, psi0=None, krylov_dim=None)[source]¶

Bases: object

Arnoldi-Krylov time evolution: e^{−iHt}|ψ₀⟩ without full diagonalisation.

The algorithm builds an m-dimensional Krylov subspace span{|ψ₀⟩, H|ψ₀⟩, H²|ψ₀⟩, …, H^{m-1}|ψ₀⟩} via the Arnoldi recurrence, then computes the matrix exponential of the small (m×m) upper Hessenberg projection. This requires only m matrix-vector products (each O(N·nnz)) instead of O(N³) for full diagonalisation.

Parameters:

  • m (int) – Krylov subspace dimension. Larger values are more accurate but more expensive. m=30 is suitable for moderate accuracy on systems with N ≤ 10⁶.

  • dt (float) – Default time step for long-time evolution (used when dt is not specified in evolve()).

Examples

>>> evolver = KrylovEvolver(m=20)
>>> psi_t = evolver.evolve(H, psi0, t=1.0)   # single step
>>> result = evolver.evolve_trajectory(H, psi0, t_max=5.0, n_steps=20)
__init__(m=30, dt=0.1, *, H=None, psi0=None, krylov_dim=None)[source]¶

imaginary_evolve(H, psi0, tau, dt=None)[source]¶

Compute e^{−Hτ}|ψ₀⟩ / ||e^{−Hτ}|ψ₀⟩||, converging to the ground state.

Repeated application of the imaginary-time propagator e^{−Hτ} damps high-energy components: at large τ only the ground state survives. The result is normalised at each step to prevent underflow.

Parameters:

  • H (Any) – Hamiltonian (same types as evolve()).

  • psi0 (ndarray) – Initial state, shape (N,). Should have non-zero overlap with the ground state.

  • tau (float) – Total imaginary time. Larger values give better convergence to the ground state.

  • dt (float | None) – Imaginary-time step. Defaults to dt.

Returns:

Normalised approximation to the ground state, shape (N,).

Return type:

np.ndarray

steady_state_reached(tol=0.0001)[source]¶

Return True if purity has converged within tol over the last 10% of the time axis.

This is a simple heuristic: if the purity varies by less than tol in the final 10% of the simulation the system is likely near its steady state.

Warning

This heuristic can give false positives for coherently driven systems whose purity is approximately constant (e.g. near-pure Rabi oscillations). It is most reliable for dissipative dynamics where purity monotonically decays to a fixed-point value.

Integrate the Lindblad equation from |0…0⟩⟨0…0|.

  • hamiltonian_terms (list[tuple[float, str]]) – Coherent Hamiltonian as a list of (coefficient, pauli_string) tuples. The Pauli string uses the format "X0", "Z0Z1", "Y2" etc. Example: [(1.0, "Z0"), (-0.5, "X0X1")].

  • jump_operators (list[JumpOperator]) – List of JumpOperator instances describing the collapse channels.

  • entanglement_cut (int) – If > 0, compute bipartite entanglement between qubits 0…(cut-1) and cut…(n-1) at every step. Entanglement data is returned in LindbladResult.entanglement. Set to 0 (default) to skip (saves memory and compute).

quantx_engine.fold_gates(ops, scale_factor)[source]¶

Amplify circuit noise by gate-level folding.

Each gate G is replaced by G·(G†·G)^k to inflate the effective noise by an integer factor (2k+1). For non-integer scale factors the last tail gates receive one additional fold so that the total gate count matches round(scale_factor * len(ops)).

Parameters:

  • ops (list[dict]) – List of gate operation dicts {"name": str, "qubits": list[int], "params": list[float]}.

  • scale_factor (float) – Desired noise amplification factor. Must be ≥ 1. Values of the form 2k+1 (odd integers) are exact; other values use partial folding.

Returns:

Folded gate sequence. Length ≈ scale_factor * len(ops).

Return type:

list[dict]

Examples

>>> ops = [{"name": "RY", "qubits": [0], "params": [0.5]}]
>>> fold_gates(ops, 3)  # G -> G·G†·G
[{"name": "RY", ...}, {"name": "RY", ..., "params": [-0.5]}, {"name": "RY", ...}]

class quantx_engine.RichardsonExtrapolator[source]¶

Bases: Extrapolator

Richardson / Lagrange extrapolation to zero noise.

Fits the unique polynomial of degree len(scale_factors) - 1 passing through all data points and evaluates it at x = 0 using the closed-form Lagrange formula. Exact for polynomial noise models of matching degree.

This is the most commonly used ZNE extrapolator: it requires no hyperparameters and works with as few as 2 points.

quantx_engine.zne_mitigate(ops, executor, scale_factors=None, extrapolator=None)[source]¶

Run zero-noise extrapolation and return the mitigated expectation value.

The circuit ops is run at each noise level (via gate folding) and the noisy results are extrapolated back to zero noise.

Parameters:

  • ops (list[dict]) – List of gate operation dicts {"name": str, "qubits": list[int], "params": list[float]}.

  • executor (Callable[[list[dict]], float]) – Callable (ops: list[dict]) -> float that runs the circuit and returns an expectation value. Build one with make_sv_executor().

  • scale_factors (list[float] | None) – Noise scale factors to evaluate. Default: [1, 3, 5]. Must all be ≥ 1; values of the form 2k+1 (odd integers) produce exact gate folding, while non-integer values use partial folding.

  • extrapolator (Extrapolator | None) – Extrapolation strategy. Default: RichardsonExtrapolator.

Return type:

ZNEResult

Examples

>>> def my_executor(ops):
...     sv = GpuStatevector(n_qubits=2)
...     for op in ops:
...         sv.apply_gate(op["name"], op["qubits"], op.get("params", ()))
...     return sv.expectation_z(0)
>>> result = zne_mitigate(bell_ops, my_executor, scale_factors=[1, 3, 5])
>>> print(result.mitigated_value)
class quantx_engine.QuasiProbabilityDecomposition(basis, gamma)[source]¶

Bases: object

Quasi-probability decomposition (QPD) of an ideal single-qubit gate.

Represents the ideal gate as a signed sum of noisy implementations:

G_ideal = Σ_i q_i * (P_i · G_noisy)

where q_i can be negative (hence “quasi-probability”) and P_i is a Pauli operator prepended before the (noisy) gate.

The one-norm γ = Σ_i |q_i| > 1 quantifies the sampling overhead; the total number of circuit samples required to achieve standard error ε scales as O(γ^{2m} / ε²) for an m-gate circuit.

Variables:

  • basis (list[tuple[str, float, float]]) – List of (pauli_name, sign, sample_prob) tuples where: - pauli_name ∈ {"I", "X", "Y", "Z"}, - sign = +1.0 or −1.0, - sample_prob = |q_i| / γ (positive, sums to 1).

  • gamma (float) – One-norm of the quasi-probability distribution.

basis: list[tuple[str, float, float]]¶
gamma: float¶
classmethod from_depolarizing(noise_prob)[source]¶

Build the QPD for a gate subject to single-qubit depolarizing noise.

Models the noisy channel as:

Λ_p(ρ) = (1-p)ρ + (p/3)(XρX + YρY + ZρZ)

and inverts it to recover the ideal gate. This is the Pauli-error parameterisation: DepolarizingNoise with probability p is (1 − p)ρ + p·I/2, which is this channel at noise_prob = 3p/4. The resulting quasi-probability weights are:

  • q_I = (1 − p/3) / (1 − 4p/3) [positive]

  • q_X = q_Y = q_Z = −(p/3) / (1 − 4p/3) [negative for p > 0]

  • γ = (1 + 2p/3) / (1 − 4p/3)

Parameters:

noise_prob (float) – Depolarizing probability p per gate, in [0, 3/4).

Raises:

MitigationError – If noise_prob is out of range.

sample(rng)[source]¶

Draw one sample from the quasi-probability distribution.

Parameters:

rng (Generator) – NumPy random generator instance.

Returns:

sign ∈ {+1.0, −1.0} and pauli_name ∈ {"I", "X", "Y", "Z"}.

Return type:

(sign, pauli_name)

quantx_engine.pec_mitigate(ops, noisy_executor, noise_prob, n_samples=100, seed=None)[source]¶

Run probabilistic error cancellation and return the mitigated expectation.

For each of the n_samples Monte Carlo trials, an independent Pauli twirl is sampled for every single-qubit gate in ops and prepended to it. The trial result is multiplied by a weight of γ^m · Π sign_i and the weighted mean over all trials converges to the noiseless expectation value.

Two-qubit gates are passed through unmodified (no twirl applied).

Parameters:

  • ops (list[dict]) – List of gate operation dicts {"name": str, "qubits": list[int], "params": list[float]}.

  • noisy_executor (Callable[[list[dict]], float]) – Callable (ops: list[dict]) -> float that runs the circuit with noise (e.g. backed by a noisy simulator or real hardware) and returns an expectation value.

  • noise_prob (float) – Single-qubit depolarizing noise probability per gate, in [0, 3/4). Used to build the quasi-probability decomposition.

  • n_samples (int) – Number of Monte Carlo samples. Larger values reduce statistical error but increase runtime. Standard error ∝ 1/√n_samples.

  • seed (int | None) – Optional random seed for reproducibility.

Return type:

PECResult

Notes

The statistical error of PEC scales as O(γ^m / √n_samples) where γ is the one-norm of the QPD and m is the number of single-qubit gates. For deep circuits this overhead becomes prohibitive, making PEC suitable mainly for shallow circuits on near-term devices.

quantx_engine.make_sv_executor(n_qubits, observable_fn, backend='numpy', dtype='complex128')[source]¶

Create a noiseless statevector executor for use with ZNE.

The returned callable initialises a fresh GpuStatevector for each circuit run, applies all gates, and returns observable_fn(sv).

Parameters:

  • n_qubits (int) – Number of qubits.

  • observable_fn (Callable[[Any], float]) – Function that takes a GpuStatevector and returns a float. Common choices: lambda sv: sv.expectation_z(0) or lambda sv: float(sv.probabilities([0])[1]).

  • backend (str) – "numpy" (default), "cupy", or "auto".

  • dtype (str) – "complex128" (default, fp64) or "complex64" (fp32).

Returns:

An executor compatible with zne_mitigate().

Return type:

Callable[[list[dict]], float]

Examples

>>> executor = make_sv_executor(2, lambda sv: sv.expectation_z(0))
>>> result = zne_mitigate(ops, executor, scale_factors=[1, 3, 5])

class quantx_engine.HardwareTranspiler(coupling_map, native_gates='cx_rz')[source]¶

Bases: object

Hardware-aware circuit transpiler.

Parameters:

  • coupling_map (CouplingMap) – Physical device topology.

  • native_gates (str | frozenset[str]) –

    Specifies the device’s native gate set. Either a string shorthand ("cx_rz", "cz_rz", "all") or a custom frozenset[str] of lower-case gate names.

    • "cx_rz" — CX/CNOT-based devices (e.g. IBM superconducting): {cx, h, x, y, z, s, sdg, t, tdg, rz, rx, ry, …}

    • "cz_rz" — CZ-based devices (e.g. Google, Rigetti): {cz, h, x, y, z, s, sdg, t, tdg, rz, rx, ry, sx, …}

    • "all" — accept all standard gates (no decomposition).

Examples

>>> dev = CouplingMap.linear(3)
>>> t = HardwareTranspiler(dev)
>>> result = t.transpile([GateOp("cx", [0, 2])])
>>> result.n_swaps
1

ρ = (1/d) ∑_{P ∈ {I,X,Y,Z}^⊗n}  Tr(P ρ) · P

to reconstruct a density matrix from its Pauli expectation values. Reconstruction is exact for noiseless (ideal) expectation values.

class quantx_engine.ProcessTomography(n_qubits=1)[source]¶

Bases: object

Quantum process tomography via the chi (χ) process matrix.

The chi matrix in the Pauli basis is defined by:

E(ρ) = ∑_{m,n}  χ_{mn}  P_m  ρ  P_n†

For a unitary channel U·ρ·U†, the chi matrix has rank 1.

Parameters:

n_qubits (int) – Number of qubits.

__init__(n_qubits=1)[source]¶

Compute the Pauli-basis chi matrix for a unitary channel U·ρ·U†.

Parameters:

unitary (ndarray) – Unitary matrix of shape (d, d) where d = 2**n_qubits.

Return type:

Chi matrix of shape (4**n_qubits, 4**n_qubits).

process_fidelity(chi1, chi2)[source]¶

Compute process fidelity F_process(E1, E2) = Tr(χ1 χ2†).

With the 1/d Pauli normalisation used by chi_matrix() this equals |⟨c1|c2⟩|² ∈ [0, 1] with 1 when the two unitaries are equal.

Parameters:

  • chi1 (ndarray) – Chi matrices of the same shape, as returned by chi_matrix().

  • chi2 (ndarray) – Chi matrices of the same shape, as returned by chi_matrix().

Return type:

Process fidelity in [0, 1].

average_gate_fidelity(chi_actual, chi_target)[source]¶

Compute average gate fidelity from chi matrices.

Uses the relation:

F_avg = (d · F_process + 1) / (d + 1)

where d = 2**n_qubits.

Parameters:

  • chi_target (ndarray) – Chi matrix of the target (ideal) gate.

Average gate fidelity in [0, 1].

class quantx_engine.GRAPESolver(H_drift, H_controls, U_target, n_steps=20, total_time=3.141592653589793, seed=None)[source]¶

Bases: object

GRAPE — Gradient Ascent Pulse Engineering.

Maximises the gate fidelity:

Φ = |Tr(U†_target U_prop)|² / d²

with respect to piecewise-constant control amplitudes u[j, k] (j = control index, k = time step index).

The gradient is computed analytically:

∂Φ/∂u_j[k] = (2 dt / d²) Im(IP* · Tr(A[k+1] H_j F[k+1]))

where F[k+1] = U_k … U_0 (forward propagator through step k), A[k+1] = U†_target · U_{n-1} … U_{k+1} (backward propagator using forward unitaries, NOT their adjoints), and IP = Tr(U†_target U_prop).

Parameters:

  • H_drift (np.ndarray) – Time-independent drift Hamiltonian, shape (d, d), Hermitian.

  • H_controls (list[np.ndarray]) – List of control Hamiltonians H_j, each shape (d, d), Hermitian.

  • U_target (np.ndarray) – Target unitary, shape (d, d).

  • n_steps (int) – Number of piecewise-constant time steps.

  • total_time (float) – Total evolution time (same units as Hamiltonian).

  • seed (int | None) – Optional seed for initial random controls.

__init__(H_drift, H_controls, U_target, n_steps=20, total_time=3.141592653589793, seed=None)[source]¶

class quantx_engine.CRABSolver(H_drift, H_controls, U_target, n_steps=20, total_time=3.141592653589793, n_harmonics=4, seed=None)[source]¶

Bases: object

CRAB — Chopped Random Basis optimal control.

Represents each control field as a sum of n_harmonics random-frequency Fourier components:

u_j(t) = ∑_k (a_k cos(ω_k t) + b_k sin(ω_k t))

where {ω_k} are drawn randomly near integer multiples of 2π/T. The scalar coefficients {a_k, b_k} are optimised by Nelder-Mead.

Parameters:

  • H_drift (np.ndarray) – Same as GRAPESolver.

  • H_controls (list[np.ndarray]) – Same as GRAPESolver.

  • U_target (np.ndarray) – Same as GRAPESolver.

  • n_steps (int) – Same as GRAPESolver.

  • total_time (float) – Same as GRAPESolver.

  • seed (int | None) – Same as GRAPESolver.

  • n_harmonics (int) – Number of Fourier harmonics per control field.

__init__(H_drift, H_controls, U_target, n_steps=20, total_time=3.141592653589793, n_harmonics=4, seed=None)[source]¶

class quantx_engine.Estimator(noise_model=None, shots=None, seed=None)[source]¶

Bases: object

Hardware-agnostic expectation-value estimator.

Computes ⟨ψ|O|ψ⟩ for each (circuit, observable) pair using a pure-NumPy statevector (noiseless) or density-matrix (noisy) simulator.

Parameters:

  • noise_model – Optional NoiseModel instance. When provided a density-matrix simulation is used; otherwise the computation is exact.

  • shots (int | None) – When positive, draw shots measurement outcomes and estimate the expectation value empirically (adds shot noise). None or 0 → exact value.

  • seed (int | None) – Random seed for reproducible shot sampling.

Example

from quantx_engine.primitives import Estimator, SparsePauliOp

bell = {
    "n_qubits": 2,
    "operations": [
        {"name": "h",  "qubits": [0]},
        {"name": "cx", "qubits": [0, 1]},
    ],
}
result = Estimator().run([bell], ["ZZ"])
# result.values ≈ [1.0]
__init__(noise_model=None, shots=None, seed=None)[source]¶
run(circuits, observables, parameter_values=None)[source]¶

Evaluate expectation values for (circuit, observable) pairs.

Parameters:

  • circuits – Single circuit or list of circuits.

  • observables – Single observable or list of observables (Pauli strings, SparsePauliOp, or PauliHamiltonian). Length must match circuits or be 1 (broadcast).

  • parameter_values – Optional list of parameter-binding dicts (one per circuit), mapping parameter name → float. May also be a single dict (applied to all circuits).

Return type:

EstimatorResult

Bases: object

Runs circuits and returns quasi-probability distributions over bitstrings.

Example

from quantx_engine.primitives import Sampler

circuit = {
    "n_qubits": 1,
    "operations": [{"name": "h", "qubits": [0]}],
}
result = Sampler(shots=1000, seed=42).run([circuit])
# result.quasi_dists[0] ≈ {0: 0.5, 1: 0.5}

repeat_until(success_cbit, success_value, body, reset_qubits=None, max_iterations=100)[source]¶

Bounded repeat-until-success (RUS) loop.

Runs the operations in body repeatedly until classical_register[success_cbit] == success_value, up to max_iterations attempts. After each failed attempt, the qubits listed in reset_qubits are reset to |0⟩ before retrying.

Parameters:

  • success_cbit (int) – Classical bit index checked for loop termination.

  • success_value (int) – Loop exits when cbits[success_cbit] == success_value.

  • body (list[dict]) – List of operation dicts (same format as self.operations).

  • reset_qubits (list[int] | None) – Qubits to reset after a failed attempt (e.g. ancilla qubits).

  • max_iterations (int) – Safety cap on the number of retries (default 100).

class quantx_engine.DynamicSimulator(noise_model=None, shots=1, seed=None)[source]¶

Bases: object

Statevector trajectory simulator for dynamic circuits.

Each shot is an independent wavefunction trajectory. Mid-circuit measurements probabilistically collapse the wavefunction; conditional gates are applied based on the resulting classical register state.

Parameters:

  • noise_model – Optional NoiseModel instance. When set, its channels act on every qubit after every gate, as on the native circuit backend (native_channels(): depolarizing, amplitude damping, bit and phase flips, T1/T2 decay). Each shot is one trajectory, so the noise is sampled as random Pauli kicks and quantum jumps and every trajectory stays a pure state.

  • shots (int) – Number of independent trajectories to run.

  • seed (int | None) – Random seed for reproducibility.

Example

circ = DynamicCircuit(2, 2).h(0).cx(0, 1).measure_all()
result = DynamicSimulator(shots=500, seed=0).run(circ)
print(result.counts)   # {"00": ~250, "11": ~250}
__init__(noise_model=None, shots=1, seed=None)[source]¶

Simulate a dynamic circuit for self.shots trajectories.

circuit (DynamicCircuit) – The DynamicCircuit to simulate.

DynamicResult

quantx_engine.hardware_efficient_ansatz(n_qubits, n_layers=1, rotation='ry')[source]¶

Hardware-efficient ansatz (HEA).

Structure per layer: 1. Single-qubit rotation (rx/ry/rz) on every qubit. 2. Entangling CNOT ladder: CX(0,1), CX(1,2), …, CX(n-2, n-1).

Repeated n_layers times, followed by a final rotation layer.

Total parameters: n_qubits * (n_layers + 1).

Parameters:

  • n_qubits (int) – Number of qubits (>= 1).

  • n_layers (int) – Number of rotation + entangling layers (>= 1).

  • rotation (str) – Single-qubit rotation gate: "rx", "ry", or "rz".

Return type:

CircuitTemplate

quantx_engine.iqp_circuit(n_qubits, depth=2, seed=None)[source]¶

Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial (IQP) circuit.

Structure (repeated depth times): 1. H on every qubit. 2. Diagonal phase layer: RZZ(theta_i_j) on random qubit pairs, then

RZ(phi_i) on each qubit.

Useful for quantum advantage demonstrations.

Parameters:

  • n_qubits (int) – Number of qubits (>= 2).

  • depth (int) – Number of H + diagonal-phase repetitions (>= 1).

  • seed (int | None) – Random seed for choosing which qubit pairs get RZZ interactions. Makes the structure reproducible.

Return type:

CircuitTemplate

quantx_engine.qaoa_circuit(n_qubits, p_layers=1)[source]¶

QAOA ansatz for MaxCut on a ring graph.

Alternating cost (ZZ Ising) and mixer (RX) layers.

Cost layer: RZZ(2*gamma_k, i, i+1) for all ring edges (i, i+1 mod n). Mixer layer: RX(2*beta_k, i) for all qubits.

Total parameters: 2 * p_layers (gamma_0…gamma_{p-1}, beta_0…beta_{p-1}).

Parameters:

  • n_qubits (int) – Number of qubits (>= 2).

  • p_layers (int) – Number of QAOA rounds (>= 1).

Return type:

CircuitTemplate

quantx_engine.ghz_circuit(n_qubits)[source]¶

GHZ state preparation circuit.

Applies H on qubit 0 followed by a CNOT ladder: CX(0,1), CX(1,2), …, CX(n-2, n-1).

No free parameters.

Parameters:

n_qubits (int) – Number of qubits (>= 2).

Return type:

CircuitTemplate

quantx_engine.quantum_fourier_transform(n_qubits, inverse=False)[source]¶

Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) or its inverse on n qubits.

Implements the standard recursive QFT decomposition: H gate + controlled-phase gates + SWAP network.

Controlled-Rz decomposition (no native CRZ gate in the simulator):

CRZ(theta, ctrl, tgt):
    RZ(theta/2, tgt)
    CX(ctrl, tgt)
    RZ(-theta/2, tgt)
    CX(ctrl, tgt)

No free parameters (fully fixed circuit).

Parameters:

  • n_qubits (int) – Number of qubits (>= 1).

  • inverse (bool) – If True, return the inverse QFT (IQFT).

Return type:

CircuitTemplate

quantx_engine.uccsd_ansatz(n_electrons, n_qubits)[source]¶

Minimal UCCSD-inspired ansatz for quantum chemistry.

Structure: 1. Hartree-Fock reference: X gates on the first n_electrons qubits

(occupying the lowest orbitals).

  1. Single excitations: For each pair (p, q) with p < n_electrons and q >= n_electrons, a parameterized RY rotation that mixes occupied and virtual orbitals.

  2. Double excitations (simplified): For each pair of single-excitation pairs ((p, q), (r, s)) taken in order, a CNOT + RZ + CNOT sequence on qubits q and s (the virtual orbitals).

This is a simplified approximation suitable for testing/demonstration, not a rigorous UCCSD implementation.

Parameters:

  • n_electrons (int) – Number of electrons (occupied orbitals). Must satisfy 1 <= n_electrons < n_qubits.

  • n_qubits (int) – Total number of spin-orbital modes (qubits). Must be >= 2.

Return type:

CircuitTemplate

class quantx_engine.NoiseCharacterizer(gate_time=0.1)[source]¶

Bases: object

Fit a parametric noise model from experimental benchmark data.

Supports fitting from:

  • fit_from_rb() — Randomized Benchmarking results

  • fit_from_xeb() — Cross-Entropy Benchmarking results

  • fit_from_process_tomography() — process chi matrices

  • fit() — combine all available sources

Parameters:

gate_time (float) – Physical gate duration in microseconds, used when estimating T1/T2 relaxation times from the fitted depolarizing probability.

__init__(gate_time=0.1)[source]¶
fit_from_rb(rb_result)[source]¶

Extract a noise model from a Randomized Benchmarking result.

Uses the single-qubit approximation:

p_dep = 2 * EPC

which is exact for a 1-qubit depolarizing channel where EPC = (d-1)/d * (1-p) with d=2.

Parameters:

rb_result – An RBResult instance.

Return type:

CharacterizedNoise

fit_from_xeb(xeb_result)[source]¶

Extract a noise model from a Cross-Entropy Benchmarking result.

Fits the exponential decay model F_XEB(d) = A * r^d via log-linear regression (np.polyfit) and estimates:

p_dep ≈ 1 - r
Parameters:

xeb_result – An XEBResult instance.

Return type:

CharacterizedNoise

fit_from_process_tomography(process_result, process_target_result=None)[source]¶

Extract a noise model from process tomography chi matrices.

Uses the relation between process infidelity and the depolarizing probability for an n-qubit system (d = 2^n):

p_dep = d**2 / (d**2 - 1) * process_infidelity
Parameters:

  • process_result – Either a ProcessTomography instance (whose chi_matrix() will be used with a provided target), or a numpy.ndarray representing a chi matrix directly.

  • process_target_result – Target chi matrix as numpy.ndarray, or None. If process_result is a numpy.ndarray, this argument is the target chi matrix used to compute process infidelity. Passing None assumes the target is an ideal (identity-like) process and uses process_infidelity = 1 - Tr(chi).

Return type:

CharacterizedNoise

fit(rb_result=None, xeb_result=None, process_chi=None, target_chi=None)[source]¶

Combine all available data sources into a single noise estimate.

If multiple sources are provided, the final depolarizing_prob is a weighted average of per-source estimates (uniform weights). The confidence is the fraction of sources whose estimates agree within a factor of 2 of the mean estimate.

At least one source must be provided.

Parameters:

  • rb_result – Optional RBResult.

  • xeb_result – Optional XEBResult.

  • process_chi – Optional chi matrix (numpy.ndarray) from process tomography.

  • target_chi – Optional target chi matrix (numpy.ndarray).

Return type:

CharacterizedNoise

quantx_engine.floquet_effective_hamiltonian(H0, H1, omega)[source]¶

First-order Floquet-Magnus effective Hamiltonian.

For H(t) = H₀ + 2 H₁ cos(ω t):

H_eff = H₀ + [H₁, H₋₁] / ω + O(1/ω²)

= H₀ + [H₁, H₁†] / ω (since H₋₁ = H₁† = H₁ for Hermitian drive)

The second term corrects for the coupling renormalisation due to the drive.

Parameters:

  • H0 (ndarray — static Hamiltonian)

  • H1 (ndarray — Fourier component at +ω (= H_drive / 2 for cos drive))

  • omega (float — drive frequency)

Return type:

ndarray — H_eff (Hermitian)

quantx_engine.driven_two_level(omega0, drive_amp, omega_drive, n_steps=200)[source]¶

Floquet spectrum of a driven two-level system.

H(t) = ω₀/2 · σz + A · cos(ω t) · σx

In the rotating frame this gives avoided crossings (Rabi model).

Parameters:

  • omega0 (float — qubit transition frequency)

  • drive_amp (float — drive amplitude)

  • omega_drive (float — drive frequency)

  • n_steps (int)

Return type:

FloquetResult

class quantx_engine.BB84Protocol(channel_error_rate=0.02, eve_intercept_fraction=0.0, detection_threshold=0.11, seed=None)[source]¶

Bases: object

Simulate the BB84 quantum key distribution protocol.

Alice encodes random bits in randomly chosen bases (rectilinear Z or diagonal X). Bob measures in randomly chosen bases. After classical sifting, only bits where bases matched are kept. Noise (channel error rate) and an optional intercept-resend eavesdropper (Eve) are modelled statistically.

Parameters:

  • channel_error_rate (float ∈ [0, 0.5]) – Intrinsic QBER from channel noise (no Eve).

  • eve_intercept_fraction (float ∈ [0, 1]) – Fraction of qubits that Eve intercepts and re-sends. Eve introduces an additional QBER of 0.25 * eve_intercept_fraction.

  • detection_threshold (float) – QBER threshold above which Eve is considered detected (default: 0.11).

  • seed (int or None)

class quantx_engine.E91Protocol(bell_pair_fidelity=0.95, channel_error_rate=0.01, seed=None)[source]¶

Bases: object

Simulate the Ekert-91 entanglement-based QKD protocol.

Alice and Bob share Bell pairs from a source. Each independently chooses among three measurement angles. Pairs where they chose the same angle contribute to the key; pairs with different angles are used to compute the CHSH S-parameter as a security test.

The channel is characterised by a Bell-pair fidelity F. Under the Werner state model, the correlation function for ideal angles is:

E(θ_A, θ_B) = -(2F − 1/2) cos(2(θ_A − θ_B))

(derived from Werner state correlations for the singlet component).

Parameters:

  • bell_pair_fidelity (float ∈ [0.25, 1]) – Fidelity of the entangled pairs shared between Alice and Bob.

  • channel_error_rate (float ∈ [0, 0.5]) – Additional bit-flip error on top of Werner-state correlations.

  • seed (int or None)

class quantx_engine.TeleportationProtocol(channel_fidelity=0.95, bsm_fidelity=0.99, seed=None)[source]¶

Bases: object

Simulate quantum state teleportation.

Alice and Bob share a Bell pair with fidelity F. Alice performs a BSM on her qubit and the input state, communicates 2 classical bits to Bob, and Bob applies the corresponding Pauli correction.

The average fidelity of the teleported state (over the Bloch sphere) is:

f_tele = (2F + 1) / 3

This exceeds the classical f = 2/3 bound iff F > 1/2.

Parameters:

  • channel_fidelity (float ∈ [0.25, 1]) – Bell-pair fidelity shared between Alice and Bob.

  • bsm_fidelity (float ∈ (0, 1]) – Alice’s BSM gate fidelity.

  • seed (int or None)

class quantx_engine.DenseCodingProtocol(channel_fidelity=0.95, seed=None)[source]¶

Bases: object

Simulate superdense coding.

Alice encodes 2 classical bits into one qubit by applying a Pauli operation to her half of a shared Bell pair, then sends the qubit to Bob. Bob performs a BSM to decode both bits.

The channel capacity in the presence of Werner-state noise F is:

C = 1 + (4F - 1)/3 · 1 + (1-(4F-1)/3) · 0
  = 1 + (4F-1)/3   [bits/qubit, approximate for Werner noise]

More precisely, the Holevo capacity of the dense coding channel is:

χ = h(F + (1-F)/4) - h((1-F)/4) * 3   [nats, Werner model]

We use the simpler error-rate model: probability of decoding error from Werner noise is (1 - (4F-1)/3) * 3/4.

Parameters:

  • channel_fidelity (float ∈ [0.25, 1]) – Bell-pair fidelity of the shared channel.

  • seed (int or None)

quantx_engine.bb84_key_rate(qber)[source]¶

Asymptotic BB84 secure key rate per sifted bit.

Uses the Shor–Preskill formula:

r = 1 - 2·h₂(QBER)

where h₂ is the binary Shannon entropy. Returns 0 if QBER ≥ 11 %.

Parameters:

qber (float ∈ [0, 0.5]) – Quantum Bit Error Rate after sifting.

Return type:

float ∈ [0, 1]

quantx_engine.chsh_inequality_value(correlations)[source]¶

Compute the CHSH S-parameter from four correlation measurements.

The CHSH inequality is S = |E(a,b) - E(a,b') + E(a',b) + E(a',b')|. Classical bound: |S| ≤ 2. Tsirelson’s quantum bound: |S| ≤ 2√2 ≈ 2.828.

Parameters:

correlations (dict mapping (alice_basis, bob_basis) → E ∈ [-1, 1]) – Must contain keys (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1).

Return type:

float (S-parameter)

quantx_engine.teleportation_fidelity(channel_fidelity)[source]¶

Average fidelity of teleported qubit state as function of channel F.

For a Werner-state channel with Bell-pair fidelity F, the average teleportation fidelity over the Bloch sphere is:

f_tele = (2F + 1) / 3

This saturates at f = 1 for F = 1 (perfect channel) and gives f = 1/2 for F = 1/4 (maximally mixed channel, same as classical guess).

Parameters:

channel_fidelity (float ∈ [0, 1])

Return type:

float ∈ [1/3, 1]

quantx_engine.fidelity_after_dephasing(F, p_deph)[source]¶

Werner fidelity after pair-level depolarising noise.

Models a two-qubit depolarising channel that with probability p_deph replaces the Bell pair with the maximally mixed state, and with probability (1 − p_deph) leaves it unchanged:

F' = (1 − p) F + p / 4

This is the exact Werner-state map for isotropic two-qubit noise with depolarising parameter p ∈ [0, 1]. Key properties:

  • p = 0 → identity (F’ = F).

  • p = 1 → fully depolarised (F’ = 1/4).

  • F = 1/4 is a fixed point for all p.

Parameters:

  • F (float ∈ [0, 1]) – Input Werner fidelity.

  • p_deph (float ∈ [0, 1]) – Two-qubit depolarising probability.

Return type:

float ∈ [0, 1]

quantx_engine.fidelity_after_swapping(F_A, F_B, F_gate=1.0)[source]¶

Fidelity after BSM-based entanglement swapping.

Given two Werner states with fidelities F_A and F_B and a BSM with fidelity F_gate, the output Werner-state fidelity is:

F_ideal = F_A · F_B + (1 − F_A)(1 − F_B) / 3
F_swap  = F_gate · F_ideal + (1 − F_gate) / 4

This is the exact formula derived from the Werner-state parameterisation p = (4F − 1)/3 and the multiplicative property p_out = p_A · p_B under a perfect BSM. Key properties:

  • F_A = 1 → F_swap = F_B (swapping a perfect pair preserves the other).

  • F_A = F_B = 1/4 → F_swap = 1/4 (maximally mixed is a fixed point).

Parameters:

  • F_A (float ∈ [0, 1]) – Fidelities of the two Bell pairs to be swapped.

  • F_B (float ∈ [0, 1]) – Fidelities of the two Bell pairs to be swapped.

  • F_gate (float ∈ [0, 1]) – BSM gate fidelity (1 = perfect BSM).

Return type:

float ∈ [0, 1]

quantx_engine.fidelity_after_purification(F, n_rounds=1)[source]¶

Fidelity after n rounds of DEJMPS entanglement purification.

Each round of DEJMPS doubles the Bell-state probability vs. depolarisation noise:

F' = F² / (F² + (1−F)²/3)
Parameters:

  • F (float ∈ [0, 1]) – Input Werner fidelity.

  • n_rounds (int) – Number of purification rounds (each round consumes one extra pair).

Return type:

float ∈ [0, 1]

class quantx_engine.SPSAOptimizer(a=0.1, c=0.1, A=10.0, alpha=0.602, gamma=0.101, seed=42)[source]¶

Bases: object

Simultaneous Perturbation Stochastic Approximation (SPSA) optimizer.

Uses only 2 function evaluations per iteration regardless of parameter count, making it efficient for noisy energy landscapes.

The gradient estimate is:

ĝ_k = [f(θ_k + c_k Δ_k) − f(θ_k − c_k Δ_k)] / (2 c_k) · Δ_k⁻¹

where Δ_k is a random ±1 Bernoulli vector (Rademacher distribution).

Update rule:

θ_{k+1} = θ_k − a_k ĝ_k
a_k = a / (A + k + 1)^α
c_k = c / (k + 1)^γ
Parameters:

  • a (float) – Initial step size numerator (controls learning rate magnitude).

  • c (float) – Initial perturbation size (should be ≈ noise level in f).

  • A (float) – Stability constant (typically set to ≈ 10 % of max_iter).

  • alpha (float) – Step-size decay exponent (theory: 0.602).

  • gamma (float) – Perturbation-size decay exponent (theory: 0.101).

  • seed (int or None) – Random seed for reproducibility.

__init__(a=0.1, c=0.1, A=10.0, alpha=0.602, gamma=0.101, seed=42)[source]¶

class quantx_engine.TDMRGResult(times, energies, entanglement_entropy, bond_dims, norms, observables, mps_final, dt, imaginary=False)[source]¶

Bases: object

Output of TDMRGSolver.

Variables:

  • times (ndarray, shape (n_steps,)) – Physical times (dt * step index).

  • energies (ndarray, shape (n_steps,)) – MPO energy expectation value ⟨H⟩ at each step.

  • entanglement_entropy (ndarray, shape (n_steps, n_sites-1)) – Von Neumann entropy S = −Σ λ² log λ² at each internal bond.

  • bond_dims (list[list[int]]) – Bond dimensions at each time step; bond_dims[t][b] is the bond dimension at bond b after step t.

  • norms (ndarray, shape (n_steps,)) – MPS norm at each step (should stay ≈ 1 for real-time, decreases for imaginary time before renormalisation).

  • observables (dict[str, ndarray]) – Per-step expectation values for user-supplied observables. Keys are observable names; values have shape (n_steps,).

  • mps_final (MPS) – State after the last time step.

  • dt (float) – Time step used.

  • imaginary (bool) – Whether imaginary-time evolution was performed.

class quantx_engine.TDMRGSolver(mpo, dt, n_steps, max_chi=32, svd_cutoff=1e-12, trotter_order=2, imaginary=False, observables=None)[source]¶

Bases: object

Time-Dependent DMRG via MPO-derived TEBD gates.

Parameters:

  • mpo (MPO) – Hamiltonian in MPO form (supports MPO.ising(), MPO.heisenberg(), or any user-built MPO).

  • dt (float) – Time step (positive; real or imaginary depending on imaginary).

  • n_steps (int) – Number of time steps.

  • max_chi (int) – Maximum bond dimension kept after each gate application.

  • svd_cutoff (float) – Singular values below this threshold are discarded.

  • trotter_order ({1, 2}) – Trotter decomposition order. Order 2 (default) uses symmetric even–odd–even splitting with half-steps on the even layer.

  • imaginary (bool) – If True perform imaginary-time evolution (convergence to ground state); re-normalises the MPS after each full sweep.

  • observables (dict[str, tuple[int, ndarray]] or None) – Optional user-defined single-site observables to track. Each entry maps an observable name to (site, operator_matrix).

Coined discrete-time quantum walk on an undirected graph.

class quantx_engine.TrotterSimulator(n_qubits, terms, initial_state=None)[source]¶

Bases: object

Hamiltonian simulation via Suzuki-Trotter product formulas.

The Hamiltonian is given as a sum of weighted Pauli strings:

H = Σ_k  c_k  P_k

The unitary exp(-iHt) is approximated by composing single-term exponentials exp(-i c_k P_k Δt) (each exact analytically) arranged according to a first-, second-, or fourth-order product formula.

Parameters:

  • n_qubits (int) – System size (≥ 1).

  • terms (sequence of TrotterTerm) – Pauli decomposition of H. Each term’s pauli_string length must equal n_qubits.

  • initial_state (np.ndarray or None) – Initial state vector of length 2**n_qubits. Defaults to the all-zero computational basis state |0…0⟩.

__init__(n_qubits, terms, initial_state=None)[source]¶
property n_qubits: int¶
property hamiltonian: ndarray¶

Full Hamiltonian matrix (read-only copy).

property initial_state: ndarray¶

Initial state vector (read-only copy).

run(t, n_steps=100, order=2, compute_exact=False)[source]¶

Simulate time evolution |ψ(t)⟩ ≈ exp(-iHt)|ψ₀⟩.

Parameters:

  • t (float) – Total simulation time. Negative values evolve backward.

  • n_steps (int) – Number of Trotter steps. Larger values give higher accuracy at proportionally larger cost.

  • order ({1, 2, 4}) – Product-formula order.

  • compute_exact (bool) – If True, compute the exact state via scipy.linalg.expm and store the error ‖ψ_trotter − ψ_exact‖₂ in the result. Requires scipy.

Return type:

TrotterResult

static trotter_error_bound(n_qubits, terms, t, n_steps, order=2)[source]¶

Compute an analytical upper bound on the Trotter error.

Uses spectral-norm commutator sums:

  • Order 1: ‖err‖ ≤ (t²/2n) Σ_{j<k} |c_j c_k| ‖[P_j,P_k]‖

  • Order 2: ‖err‖ ≤ (t³/12n²) Σ_{j,k,j≠k} |c_j² c_k| ‖[[P_j,P_k],P_j]‖

  • Order 4: rough bound via ‖H‖⁵ t⁵ / (120 n⁴)

Parameters:

  • n_qubits (int) – Same semantics as run().

  • terms (Sequence[TrotterTerm]) – Same semantics as run().

  • t (float) – Same semantics as run().

  • n_steps (int) – Same semantics as run().

  • order (int) – Same semantics as run().

Returns:

Non-negative error bound.

Return type:

float

static optimal_steps(n_qubits, terms, t, target_error=0.001, order=2)[source]¶

Return the minimum n_steps whose error bound ≤ target_error.

Uses binary search over trotter_error_bound().

class quantx_engine.SYKModel(N=None, q=4, seed=None, *, n_sites=None)[source]¶

Bases: object

Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev random q-body Majorana fermion Hamiltonian.

The q=4 SYK model is the minimal model conjectured to have a holographic (AdS₂) dual at low temperatures; it exhibits maximal quantum chaos.

The Hamiltonian is:

H = (i^{q/2} / q!) Σ_{i₁<…<i_q} J_{i₁…i_q} γ_{i₁}…γ_{i_q}

where γ_i are Majorana fermion operators satisfying {γ_i, γ_j} = 2δ_{ij}, mapped to qubits via the Jordan-Wigner transformation.

Parameters:

  • N (int) – Number of Majorana modes (must be even). The qubit system has N//2 qubits; the Hilbert space has dimension 2^{N//2}.

  • q (int) – Body count (must be even, typically 4).

  • seed (int or None) – Random seed for reproducibility.

quantx_engine.compute_otoc(hamiltonian, op_w, op_v, site_w, site_v, t, n_qubits, initial_state=None, n_steps=100, use_trotter=False)[source]¶

Compute the OTOC F(t) = ⟨ψ|W†(t) V† W(t) V|ψ⟩.

The scrambling diagnostic is C(t) = 1 − Re F(t).

For a thermalising system C(t) grows from 0 to ~1 on the scrambling time scale; for an integrable system it stays near 0.

Parameters:

  • hamiltonian (np.ndarray) – (2^n × 2^n) Hermitian Hamiltonian matrix.

  • op_w (str) – Single-site Pauli operators ('X', 'Y', 'Z', or 'I').

  • op_v (str) – Single-site Pauli operators ('X', 'Y', 'Z', or 'I').

  • site_w (int) – Qubit indices for W and V respectively.

  • site_v (int) – Qubit indices for W and V respectively.

  • t (float) – Time of evolution.

  • n_qubits (int) – System size (used to build operator matrices).

  • initial_state (np.ndarray or None) – State |ψ⟩ in which expectation value is taken. Defaults to |0…0⟩.

  • n_steps (int) – Trotter steps (only used when use_trotter=True).

  • use_trotter (bool) – If True, approximate exp(-iHt) via second-order Trotter; otherwise use scipy.linalg.expm (exact, requires scipy).

Return type:

OTOCResult

quantx_engine.dmrg_2d(Lx, Ly, J=1.0, bond_dim=16, sweeps=4, model='heisenberg')[source]¶

Ground-state DMRG for the 2D Heisenberg (or Ising) model on an Lx×Ly lattice.

Uses a snake-path MPS mapping to convert the 2D problem to 1D, then runs two-site DMRG sweeps. The 1D chain has Lx*Ly sites with both short-range (adjacent on snake path) and medium-range (cross-row) bonds.

Parameters:

  • Lx (int) – Lattice dimensions. Total sites = Lx * Ly.

  • Ly (int) – Lattice dimensions. Total sites = Lx * Ly.

  • J (float) – Exchange coupling (positive = antiferromagnetic).

  • bond_dim (int) – Maximum MPS bond dimension (controls accuracy).

  • sweeps (int) – Number of DMRG sweeps (left-to-right + right-to-left = one sweep).

  • model ({'heisenberg', 'ising'}) – ‘heisenberg’: H = J Σ (XX + YY + ZZ) ‘ising’: H = -J Σ ZZ

Return type:

DMRG2DResult

class quantx_engine.CachedDMRG(mpo, max_chi=32, eps=1e-10, n_sweeps=10, tol=1e-08, seed=None)[source]¶

Bases: object

DMRG with cached environment tensors for O(N) per-sweep complexity.

The standard DMRG rebuilds the left-environment from scratch during the right-to-left pass (_build_left_env_to, O(N) cost per site → O(N²) total). This variant retains the left-environment stack built during the left-to-right pass and reads from it during the right-to-left pass.

Parameters:

  • mpo (MPO) – Hamiltonian.

  • max_chi (int) – Hard bond-dimension cap.

  • eps (float) – Relative SVD truncation threshold for adaptive bond dimension. If None, fall back to fixed max_chi truncation.

  • n_sweeps (int) – Maximum number of left+right sweeps.

  • tol (float) – Convergence threshold on the per-sweep energy change.

  • seed (int | None) – Random seed for the initial MPS.

quantx_engine.ghz_fidelity(n_qubits, max_bond=2, eps=1e-12)[source]¶

Fidelity of an MPS-prepared GHZ state vs the exact GHZ state.

The GHZ circuit is: H on qubit 0, then CNOT(i, i+1) for i = 0 … n-2. The exact GHZ state has bond dimension 2 everywhere, so max_bond=2 is sufficient for lossless representation.

Parameters:

  • n_qubits (int) – Number of qubits (works for n ≥ 1, useful at n = 50).

  • max_bond (int) – MPS bond dimension cap.

  • eps (float) – Relative SVD truncation threshold.

Returns:

Fidelity F = |⟨GHZ_exact | GHZ_MPS⟩|² ∈ [0, 1].

Return type:

float

class quantx_engine.StabilizerState(n_qubits)[source]¶

Bases: object

Aaronson-Gottesman binary symplectic tableau for n-qubit stabilizer states.

Tableau layout (following [AG04] Section 4)¶

Row indices 0..n-1 : destabilizer generators Row indices n..2n-1 : stabilizer generators Column layout per row: [x_0, …, x_{n-1}, z_0, …, z_{n-1}, r]

where x_i, z_i ∈ {0,1} and r ∈ {0,1} is the phase (r=1 means −1 factor).

All Clifford gates are O(n) vectorized numpy operations (no Python loops).

param n_qubits:

Number of qubits. The tableau shape is (2n) × (2n+1).

int

class quantx_engine.FTQCPipeline(code_distance, p_physical, p_meas=0.0, decoder='mwpm')[source]¶

Bases: object

End-to-end fault-tolerant QC pipeline for a single logical qubit.

Simulates the full error-correction cycle:

  1. Encode logical |0⟩ (or |1⟩) using a distance-d surface code.

  2. Inject independent depolarizing noise on each data qubit per round.

  3. Extract stabilizer syndromes (optionally with measurement errors).

  4. Decode with MWPM (or greedy) to get a Pauli correction.

  5. Determine whether a logical error occurred.

Parameters:

  • code_distance (int) – Surface code distance d (must be ≥ 3, odd recommended).

  • p_physical (float) – Physical error rate per qubit per error-correction round (0 < p < 0.5).

  • p_meas (float, default 0.0) – Syndrome measurement error probability per stabilizer per round. Set to 0 for the ideal code-capacity noise model.

  • decoder ({"mwpm", "greedy"}, default "mwpm") – Syndrome decoder. "mwpm" uses minimum-weight perfect matching; "greedy" uses the built-in greedy matching in SurfaceCode.

__init__(code_distance, p_physical, p_meas=0.0, decoder='mwpm')[source]¶
run(n_shots=1000, n_rounds=1, seed=None)[source]¶

Run a Monte Carlo simulation of the error-correction pipeline.

Parameters:

  • n_shots (int) – Number of independent trials.

  • n_rounds (int) – Syndrome extraction rounds per trial. Use n_rounds=1 for the ideal code-capacity model; use larger values with p_meas > 0 for the phenomenological noise model.

  • seed (int | None) – Random seed for reproducibility.

PipelineResult
